lessons.title: Unsoundness: definitions, examination and grading
lessons.html:
What unsoundness means

A horse is unsound when it has a condition that affects, or is likely to affect, its ability to perform its intended use. Unsoundness includes lameness, but also wind problems, eye conditions and some conformational defects. A blemish, by contrast, is a cosmetic mark such as a healed scar or a cold splint that does not affect function. At NQF level 5 you must recognise conditions, interpret their significance for purpose and value, and know when to refer to a veterinarian. Diagnosis and treatment remain the vet's responsibility.

The lameness examination

  1. History: onset, duration, work, shoeing, previous injuries and treatments.
  2. Observation at rest: stance, weight shifting, pointing a foot, muscle wastage, swellings.
  3. Palpation: feel each limb from top to bottom for heat, swelling, pain and digital pulses; use hoof testers on the sole.
  4. Movement: walk and trot in a straight line on a firm surface, then lunge on hard and soft ground in both directions.
  5. Flexion tests: the vet holds a joint flexed for a set time, then trots the horse off to see if lameness worsens.
  6. Diagnostic tools: nerve blocks, radiographs, ultrasound and scintigraphy, used by the vet to localise and confirm.

Reading the signs

  • Forelimb lameness: the head rises when the lame leg lands and drops when the sound leg lands.
  • Hindlimb lameness: the hip on the lame side rises more (hip hike) or has a greater range of movement; shortened stride.
  • Lameness that worsens on a circle on hard ground often points to lower-limb or foot pain; worse on soft ground may point to soft-tissue problems.

Grading lameness

A commonly used 0 to 5 scale (AAEP):

GradeDescription
0No lameness detected
1Difficult to see, inconsistent
2Difficult to see at walk or straight trot, consistent under certain conditions
3Consistently seen at trot
4Obvious at walk
5Minimal weight bearing or unable to move

lessons.title: Conditions of the foot and lower limb
lessons.html:
Foot conditions

ConditionFeaturesSignificance
LaminitisInflammation of the laminae; rocked-back stance, heat, bounding pulse; possible rotation or sinking of the pedal boneEmergency; chronic cases may limit use permanently
Navicular syndromeChronic heel pain in the forelimbs, often bilateral; short, choppy stride, worse on hard circlesManaged with farriery and vet care; affects performance and value
Pedal osteitisInflammation and demineralisation of the pedal bone, often from concussionRecurrent lameness on hard ground
SideboneOssification of the collateral cartilagesOften a blemish unless associated with lameness
Abscess, seedy toe, quittorInfection in the hoof; acute severe lameness with abscessUsually resolves with drainage and care; quittor is more serious

Bone and joint conditions

  • Ringbone: new bone around the pastern or coffin joint. High ringbone affecting the pastern joint is significant; non-articular ringbone may be less so.
  • Splints: bony enlargements on the splint bones; cause lameness when forming ("hot") but are often only a blemish once cold, unless they interfere with the suspensory ligament or knee.
  • Bone spavin: osteoarthritis of the lower hock joints; stiffness, toe dragging, positive hock flexion. Common cause of hindlimb lameness in older sport horses.
  • Osteochondrosis (OCD): developmental cartilage defects in young horses, often in the stifle, hock or fetlock, with joint swelling.
  • Sesamoiditis and fractures: significant, require imaging.

Soft-tissue conditions

  • Tendinitis (bowed tendon): injury to the superficial digital flexor tendon; heat, swelling, bowed profile behind the cannon. Requires long rest and controlled rehabilitation; risk of re-injury.
  • Suspensory desmitis: injury to the suspensory ligament; common in sport and racehorses.
  • Bog spavin and windgalls: soft, fluid swellings of the hock joint or fetlock tendon sheath; often blemishes unless lame.
  • Curb: swelling at the back of the hock below the point, linked to sickle hocks.

lessons.title: Other unsoundness and applying the knowledge
lessons.html:
Wind, eyes and neurological conditions

  • Laryngeal hemiplegia (roaring): paralysis of the left side of the larynx; a roaring noise at fast work; limits racing and eventing. Diagnosed by endoscopy.
  • Equine asthma (heaves/RAO): chronic cough, heave line, exercise intolerance; managed by dust-free environment and vet treatment.
  • Eye conditions: cataracts, recurrent uveitis and corneal scars can affect vision and safety.
  • Wobbler syndrome and other neurological conditions: incoordination, a serious safety issue for riders.
  • Stereotypies such as crib-biting and weaving are vices, often declared at sale because they affect value.

Applying knowledge in practice

Pre-purchase examinations

A vet performs a structured examination before a sale. Your role is to understand the findings and advise on suitability for the buyer's purpose. A small splint may be irrelevant for a trail horse but significant for a show hunter judged on appearance. A grade 1 hindlimb lameness may be acceptable in a light-use pleasure horse but not in a high-level dressage horse.

Daily management

  • Run legs down daily to detect heat and swelling early.
  • Trot up horses regularly on a firm surface.
  • Keep records of findings, vet reports, imaging and treatments.
  • Adjust work, footing and farriery to prevent problems: avoid excessive work on hard ground, keep feet balanced, warm up and cool down properly.

Rehabilitation

Follow the vet's rehabilitation plan exactly: box rest, controlled hand walking, gradual increases in work, rechecks and scans. Rushing return to work is a major cause of re-injury.

Ethics and welfare

Never mask lameness with medication before a sale, competition or examination. Under the Animals Protection Act 71 of 1962, working a horse that is unfit because of lameness or illness can amount to cruelty. Declare known conditions honestly.

Key points

  • Unsoundness affects function; a blemish is cosmetic only.
  • A systematic exam covers history, observation, palpation, movement and flexion, with vet diagnostics.
  • Head nod indicates forelimb lameness; hip hike indicates hindlimb lameness.
  • Know key foot, bone, joint and soft-tissue conditions and their significance.
  • Judge significance against the horse's intended purpose.
  • Follow rehabilitation plans and never mask lameness.
